newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FEATURE - Labour approach on NZ Reserve Bank seen as workable.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Labour approach on NZ Reserve Bank seen as workable.

text.p: Financial markets would not fear for the future of New Zealand's independent central bank -- hailed as a model worldwide -- under a left-wing coalition, as long as the Labour Party which created it was at the helm, according to economists.

The system of a fiercely autonomous bank and governor bound by contract to adhere to strict anti-inflation policies free of political interference has made New Zealand the darling of world free-market economists since it was introduced in 1989.

But with elections on October 12 under a new proportional representation system which favours minority or coalition governments, there is doubt over whether a new government would persevere with the tough, often unpopular, monetary policies which have brought low inflation but, critics say, cost jobs.

The main opposition Labour Party which introduced the 1989 Reserve Bank Act has said it is still committed to the core element of the policy which is price stability. It would, however, widen the target range for underlying inflation to minus one to three percent from the current tight limits of zero to two percent.

Economists say they could live with that but are more concerned at other opposition parties' proposals which would add politically charged factors like growth and jobs to the list of objectives under which the Reserve Bank must set policy.

"There are fundamental difficulties in (the Reserve Bank of New Zealand) having a range of targets and objectives. Monetary policy is effectively only one tool. How you use one tool for multiple objectives is conceptually very difficult to reconcile," said Paul Stewart, chief economist at the Australia and New Zealand Banking Group.

"Financial markets' reaction to changes of that nature would be quite negative. There would be a perception that significantly higher rates of inflation were going to be tolerated, and that would increase risk premium in interest rates, particularly in long term interest rates," he said.
CENTRAL BANK FREE FROM INTERFERENCE
The absence of political interference has given New Zealand monetary policy credibility and underpinned a whole raft of radical economic free market reforms over the past six years.

But the other two main opposition parties, the left-wing Alliance and economic nationalist New Zealand First, want the objectives of the Reserve Bank Act (RBA) widened to include growth. The Alliance also wants employment included as a factor.

Financial markets have been spooked by the economic policies of the Alliance and New Zealand First which have been perceived as a step back from the path of economic reform. Economists said their policies on the RBA were no exception.
"I just don't see that it is a workable solution," said AMP economist Peter Scobie. "The Reserve Bank would be much better to concentrate on delivering a low inflation environment."

Opinion polls show the election finely balanced but suggest the parties of the left and centre-left are set to win a narrow majority over the conservative National Party government and its potential partners on the right.
The economists said a left-wing coalition would not cause too much of a fracas in the markets provided Labour headed it.

"Labour policy on the whole is fairly sensible and transparent, so in that respect I don't think it holds too many fears for financial markets. Plus (finance spokesman) Michael Cullen would appear to be a sensible finance minister," said Scobie.
ALLIANCE AND NZ FIRST WORRY MARKETS
Latest polls show Labour cementing second place behind National at around 20 percent. National has around 38, while NZ First and the Alliance hover around 16 and 13 respectively.
Doyle Paterson Brown economist Stephen Toplis said of all economic structures, the Reserve Bank framework was the least under pressure from the potential change in government.

"Fundamentally, both National and Labour support the Reserve Bank Act. They may have slightly different views on its interpretation and implementation, but fundamentally they back it. As a consequence I can't see any major threat to that Act."
He said that if NZ First or the Alliance were to lead a coalition, the exact wording in the Act of any expansion in the Reserve Bank's objectives would be crucial to market reaction.

The Alliance wants the central bank to target employment and "sustainable well-being" in the economy. Toplis said the Reserve Bank probably believed its current target aimed for sustainable well-being through low inflation.

"Although reading between the lines, one suspects that the Alliance would direct the Reserve Bank more actively to target growth. If that is the case, that would be considered unequivocably negative," he said.
"What would generate a major panic is if they said something like "Target 0-2 percent inflation and three percent employment growth.' That would be a real worry."
Toplis said markets were alarmed by NZ First's proposal to replace the 0-2 percent target with the aim of running inflation marginally below that of New Zealand's trading partners.

"It's scary, particularly when you consider who those trading partners are...If you take our top 10 trading partners, quite a few of those are Asian nations, which are prone to moderately high rates of inflation," he said.

The economists agreed Labour's proposal to widen the underlying inflation target band to minus one to three percent was not cause for concern. Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash has said he could work with a wider target.
Scobie said a wider band would give the Bank more flexibility in managing monetary policy through an economic cycle, and lessen the chance of it over-correcting in response to economic indicators.
Stewart said the central bank might respond more slowly to a build-up in inflationary pressures, "so that inflation pressures by the time they do react are more embedded".
Toplis also cautioned that problems could arise if people interpreted the widening as a softening in monetary policy.
"Then you could argue that we would end up with higher average rates of inflation, and that would be perceived as negative," he said.
